rv.q: Hall’s play is funny, serious, sad and stirring: a rich, absorbing drama that tells a story well but that is also galvanised throughout by the author’s passionate belief in the importance of culture and learning for all.
This is a wonderful play about art in people’s lives and dreams, and the difference it makes to them.
Somewhere in this mass of material lurks a brilliant play but, like the terrorist mastermind, it hasn't been winkled out yet.

It all proves so well acted – and so heartfelt, so honest, so funny and so disarmingly clever – that while this West End run marks the end of the play’s second national tour there must surely be more to come.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this true story of working-class miners-turned-artists, praising its heartening tale and persuasive argument for art's accessibility, though one dissenter finds it less compelling than its acclaimed reputation suggests.
